primitives.name: Blocking Effort
primitives.verbatim_quote: The object of football is to score points and no team is able to do this unless the backs receive the protection they have a right to expect from the men who are playing in the line.
primitives.assumptions: Linear relationship between line blocker effort and runner protection; static game state assumption.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When E_b < threshold, P_r approaches zero.

layer2.mapping: E_b = f(arm_position, shoulder_contact, hip_stability) maps to P_r via inverse kinematic constraints.
layer2.telemetry: Runner proximity to line after snap

primitives.name: Blocking Method
primitives.verbatim_quote: There are two methods of blocking an opponent, although these two permit of numerous variations.
primitives.assumptions: Exclusive binary choice between M_s and M_h; variation is deterministic within method.
primitives.breakdown_regime: M_s = 1 implies M_h = 0 and vice versa.

layer2.mapping: M_s and M_h are isomorphic to angular momentum vectors in collision dynamics.
layer2.telemetry: Angle of contact vector relative to opponent axis

primitives.name: Contact Point
primitives.verbatim_quote: Opponents can be blocked with the shoulder or with the hip.
primitives.assumptions: Contact points are fixed geometric locations; no deformation occurs.
primitives.breakdown_regime: C_s ≠ C_h due to anatomical constraints.

layer2.mapping: C_s and C_h define moment arms in torque calculation against opponent force vector.
layer2.telemetry: Distance between contact point and opponent's center of mass

primitives.name: Blocking Velocity
primitives.verbatim_quote: The blocker should, the moment the ball is snapped, jump into his opponent, striking him squarely with the shoulder, if possible.
primitives.assumptions: Instantaneous reaction time; constant acceleration during approach phase.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \vec{v}_b exceeds opponent's speed, contact becomes effective.

layer2.mapping: \vec{v}_b corresponds to impulse transfer rate in Newtonian mechanics.

Blocking in football operates as a dual constraint system: one optimizing for defensive integrity (protecting backs) and another for offensive disruption (preventing gaps). Each primitive contributes to a composite objective function where E_b = f(M_s, M_h, C_s, C_h, v_b). The derivation begins with the fundamental principle that protection is a function of line blocker engagement, which is quantified through contact geometry and temporal dynamics. The blocking method defines the geometric framework, while contact point determines leverage. Velocity introduces kinetic energy into the system. These components form a vector space where each dimension represents a tactical variable. Failure modes occur when any component violates physical or rule-bound limits—such as arm-blocking being classified as holding or insufficient velocity leading to missed tackles. Dualities emerge in the trade-off between shoulder vs hip contact: shoulder offers greater linear momentum but less stability, whereas hip provides more stable base but lower impulse. This creates a Pareto frontier of optimal blocking strategies.
